*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray $N$, i.e., $O(N)$.
Early ray termination can reduce the average number of samples processed, especially in dense volumes.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ per ray, as only the accumulator state is needed.
*   **Measured Performance:** Performance depends heavily on the volume density and the effectiveness of early ray termination.
In sparse volumes, performance is similar to back-to-front methods.
In dense volumes, front-to-back compositing with early termination is significantly faster.
*   **Strengths:** Physically plausible results for participating media; supports early ray termination; simple to implement.
*   **Limitations:** Order-dependent (non-commutative); requires samples to be ordered along the ray; early ray termination is not possible with back-to-front compositing.
*   **When to use:** Standard direct volume ray casting where semi-transparency and internal structure visualization are required.

*   **When not to use:** When maximum intensity projection (MIP) or average projection is desired; when samples are not available in ray order and hardware acceleration for unordered accumulation is not available.
Compositing in volume rendering originated with the development of direct volume ray casting techniques in the early 1990s.
The front-to-back compositing equation is derived from the volume rendering integral, which models the interaction of light with participating media.
The method has been widely adopted in scientific visualization and medical imaging due to its ability to render semi-transparent structures effectively.
